transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-20
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Evan (Redwood SE), Sofia (Redwood CSM), Liam (Orion CTO), Priya (Lead ML Eng), Daniel (Platform Eng)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Orion is evaluating Redwood for a mix of hosted and Dedicated options. Main priorities: easy SDK integrations (LangChain/LlamaIndex), gateway/proxy requirements, rate limits and quotas, and observability hooks for SLOs and cost monitoring. Security (SSO, KMS, SOC2) is a blocker for Private/Dedicated decisions. Next steps: share pricing, integration docs, run a short benchmark POC.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, appreciate the time. can we do quick intros? i'm maya, account lead at redwood.
[00:12] Liam: Liam here, cto at orion. We've got priya and daniel from engineering.
[00:17] Priya: hi all.
[00:19] Daniel: hey.
[00:20] Evan: Evan, solutions engineer, i'll drive the technical bits. Sofia from csm on the line.

[00:31] Maya: quick agenda — understand your stack and integration needs, constraints (security, latency, cost), then talk about how our hosted/dedicated/private options map, and next steps. sound good?
[00:40] Liam: yes. Our immediate goal is integrating LLM features into two products: "search assist" and "document summarization". We need low latency for search assist (sub-300ms p95 ideally) and cost predictability for summarization at scale.

[01:05] Priya: technical context: we currently use a mix of in-house microservices and third-party APIs. we have an API gateway layer (kong right now) and are exploring embedding LangChain/llamaindex in our pipelines. main questions: what SDKs you support, examples for langchain/llamaindex, and whether we can run a proxy/gateway to route requests to dedicated nodes.

[01:32] Evan: absolutely. Redwood provides official SDKs in python and js, and we have sample connectors for LangChain and LlamaIndex. i'll send a repo with examples — it's fairly straightforward: a small adapter that wraps our streaming client and fits into chains. we also have examples for using a local gateway/proxy to multiplex traffic or add auth.

[01:50] Priya: are those adapters opinionated? we don't want to rework our chains drastically.

[01:56] Evan: they're intentionally lightweight. you can drop in a single class that implements call and stream semantics. for llamaindex we have a loader pattern example and a few prompt template helpers, but nothing that forces a particular architecture.

[02:18] Daniel: about gateway — we want to put a reverse proxy in front that does rate limiting and quota enforcement, possibly transforms headers for tenant ids. any gotchas?

[02:28] Evan: that's a common pattern. two options: 1) route through your gateway to our hosted API (we recommend adding per-tenant tokens or headers), or 2) if Dedicated or Private, you can host the gateway inside the same VPC and talk directly to the private endpoint. rate limiting you can enforce at the gateway, and we also support per-key quotas on our side. when you use dedicated, you can configure reserved capacity to avoid noisy neighbor issues.

[02:58] Liam: ok, and about observability — we need token-level cost breakdowns, per-route latency, and tracing to our X-Ray/Datadog stack. how mature are those hooks?

[03:10] Evan: we expose per-request metadata in logs and offer ingestion hooks for trace IDs. we can forward structured events to your tracing system via our exporters, and the console has token-level cost/latency breakdowns and per-model dashboards. there are also hooks for custom labels you can pass in the SDK calls.

[03:36] Priya: that sounds good, any latency overhead for those labels/tracing?

[03:41] Evan: negligible — labels are passed as metadata, not in the critical data path. the runtime is optimized for low overhead; biggest factors are model choice, batching window, and networking.

[04:05] Daniel: for search assist we're worried about p95 under load. do you have any numbers or benchmark patterns?

[04:12] Evan: yes — we typically publish profiles for our curated models. for example, a 13B quantized variant on a dedicated A100-equivalent pool gives ~120-200ms p95 for 512 tokens with continuous batching tuned. that said, your actual numbers depend on prompt length, KV-cache hit rates, and concurrency. for sub-300ms p95 we recommend Dedicated with prefix caching enabled for search-like work.

[04:43] Liam: prefix caching? can you explain, i might have heard it slightly different.

[04:47] Evan: sure — prefix or KV caching stores encoded key/value states for repeated prefixes, so for short prompts like "user query + doc snippet" you can avoid recomputing the full context every time. it's a big win for interactive search where many requests share prefixes.

[05:08] Priya: that implies stateful nodes. does that complicate autoscaling?

[05:14] Evan: the runtime manages KV cache placement and rebalances; autoscaling is aware of cache warmness. we can discuss warm-up strategies — we also offer a cache pre-warm API for common prefixes.

[05:34] Maya: circling back to security — Liam, you flagged SOC2 and SSO as blockers?

[05:40] Liam: yes. for any Dedicated/Private deployment we need SOC2 type 2, SAML SSO integration with Okta, and KMS-backed key management in the VPC. also audit logs retained for 1 year.

[05:54] Sofia: we have SOC2 docs and an enterprise security pack. For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS/HSM and audit log forwarding to your s3/secure bucket. SAML/SSO is supported (Okta, Azure AD) and RBAC hooks. i'll attach those docs.

[06:12] Priya: good. what about data residency? we have european customers and need to ensure data stays in eu-west region for certain tenants.

[06:20] Maya: we support region pinning for hosted and dedicated — you can route EU tenants to EU-backed clusters. For Private it's in your VPC so you control residency.

[06:33] Daniel: on quotas: we need to enforce per-customer quotas and throttling to avoid noisy tenants. you mentioned per-key quotas — do you support dynamic update of quotas via API?

[06:43] Evan: yes, quotas are configurable via our control plane API; you can update them programmatically, and there's also a webhook for quota breach events so your gateway can respond.

[06:58] Liam: about cost management, we want to estimate unit cost for summarization pipeline — high token volumes, batch-friendly. how would you recommend low cost without big latency impact?

[07:09] Evan: batching and quantized models are the levers. for non-interactive jobs like bulk summarization, use larger batches and more aggressive quantized variants; we can suggest quantization profiles tuned for your accuracy/latency tradeoff. Redwood Optimize can run a small evaluation across prompts and recommend model + quantization choices.

[07:35] Priya: do you have a prebuilt integration for our internal data pipeline? we feed docs through a kafka cluster.

[07:42] Evan: we have connectors and example architectures for Kafka-based ingestion — usually a consumer writes prompts to a worker pool which calls Redwood's SDK; for throughput we recommend our batching endpoints or using our streaming API if you want partial outputs early.

[07:59] Daniel: request from infra: we'll likely front with our gateway and send authenticated requests to your hosted endpoint. if we go dedicated, can we keep the same code path and only swap endpoints?

[08:09] Evan: yes, that's one of our design goals — same SDK and API surface across hosted/dedicated/private. you mostly change base URL and credentials; rollout policies and capacity settings differ but client code stays the same.

[08:28] Liam: any known gotchas integrating with LangChain or LlamaIndex? latency behavior when streaming?

[08:36] Evan: LangChain's abstractions are sometimes built around sync calls. for streaming we provide async adapters. LlamaIndex often expects a specific retriever pattern — our example shows how to plug the SDK as a LanguageModel class. the biggest thing is to make sure your chain handles partial streaming tokens and timeouts gracefully.

[08:56] Priya: ok. about SLA and uptime — Dedicated offers SLA?

[09:02] Maya: Dedicated comes with an SLA for uptime and latency SLOs; private deployments have customizable support tiers. we'll share the SLA doc.

[09:10] Liam: for POC we'd probably start with Hosted (fast) to validate flows then move to Dedicated for production. would you recommend starting POC on Hosted or directly on Dedicated?

[09:21] Evan: depends on how critical isolation/latency is. recommended flow we see: quick integration and functional POC on Hosted (fastest time to value), then a short Dedicated pilot to validate p95 latency and cost at scale. we can do a 30-day Dedicated pilot with reserved capacity for benchmarking.

[09:40] Daniel: one last infra question — can we run a local gateway that signs requests and rotates keys without exposing tokens?

[09:48] Evan: yes, commonly we see a gateway that injects tenant ids and signs or mints short-lived credentials via our token service. we support short-lived tokens and key rotation APIs.

[09:59] Priya: any limitations on number of connections from gateway to Redwood? we have spikes during product launches.

[10:05] Evan: we support high concurrency; for very high qps we suggest pooling connections and using our batch endpoints to reduce per-request overhead. Dedicated has capacity planning options and autoscaling/burst capacity to handle spikes.

[10:20] Maya: ll let's capture remaining open items and next steps — we've flagged security docs, pricing, LangChain examples, and a benchmark dataset from you.

[10:29] Liam: yep. we'll pull together a sample workload — around 15k qps peak across shards? that's a rough number — Daniel will generate a detailed traffic profile.

[10:40] Daniel: i'll share the traffic and token distribution, plus a list of tenant residency requirements.

[10:47] Priya: can we also get an example of the observability pane — token-level cost breakdown exports? we want to wire that into our internal billing.

[10:56] Evan: i'll export a sample report and show the API for cost exports.

[11:04] Maya: great. Sophia will attach SOC2 and the enterprise security pack, and we'll follow up on scheduling. anything else?

[11:12] Liam: no, thanks everyone. good session.

[11:15] Maya: thanks all — we'll send the notes and links.

End of call.
